answers.U1-S1: Seeing flamingos for the first time at age six, on a walk to a river, gave the narrator a delight that no later sighting ever equalled.
answers.U1-S2: He was very young and timid, not yet confident on the plain; he only agreed once his brother promised to avoid any cattle.
answers.U1-S3: To show how long and tiring the walk was for a six-year-old, with detours and tall grass making the journey hard.
answers.U1-S4: Slowly and gravely, with a dignified, serious, deliberate manner.
answers.U1-S5: Because the open wings revealed a glorious crimson colour he had not seen while they were folded, making the bird seem even more beautiful.
answers.U1-S6: The birds were unusual for the area, never seen there before; flamingos did not normally visit their small water-courses, so the sighting was rare.
answers.U1-S7: Its tall white-and-rose body and spreading crimson wings seemed so beautiful and otherworldly to the child that it looked heavenly, like an angel.
answers.U1-S8: The first sight came when he was a small child seeing something new, strange and unexpected; that freshness and childhood wonder could never be repeated.
answers.U1-S9: It moves forward to his many later sightings, then contrasts them with the first, emphasizing that the childhood experience remained unmatched.
answers.U1-S10: Fond, nostalgic appreciation; he treasures the memory and still regards that first sight as his greatest delight in the bird.
